processing: Leaves, bark and twigs of the Combretum micranthum shrub are harvested and sold in bundles, then steeped or brewed strong in boiling water.
harvest_season: Harvested and sold during the dry season leading up to and during Ramadan.
appearance_dry: Bundles of dried brownish-green leaves with twigs and bark.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear amber to reddish brown when brewed strong.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark brown-green leaves with hard twig pieces.
taste_profile: Few reliable tasting accounts exist; as usually served, strong and herbal, softened by sugar and milk.

brewing.notes: Brew it strong in boiling water. The traditional way to serve it is with sugar and milk, alongside bread.

vintage_note: Not sold by year. In West Africa it appears in market bundles in the dry season, with most demand around Ramadan. Elsewhere it is sold dried by import shops; choose whole leaf and check for a recent packing date.
description:
Kinkeliba is the tea of Combretum micranthum, a shrub of West African hills and tiger bush, known by this name in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea, Benin and the Gambia. It is called sekhew in Wolof and ŋɔlɔbɛ in Bambara.

There is nothing elaborate in the making. Leaves, bark and twigs are gathered, sold in bundles and brewed in boiling water, as a traditional tonic drink of the tropical savanna.

Its place at the table says most: among West African Muslims, particularly Wolof, Fula and Mandinka communities, it is brewed strong and mixed with sugar and milk, then drunk with bread at sundown to break the Ramadan fast. Try it that way before judging it plain.

Season shapes the market, with the bundles appearing in the dry season ahead of Ramadan. It has traditional medicinal uses as well, including a root decoction against Guinea worm, but those are folk uses, and that decoction is not this tea.
history:
The name is believed to come from the Fulani language. Little is documented about when the tea entered daily use, beyond its standing as a traditional drink across the savanna countries.

The best recorded custom is its role during Ramadan among West African Muslims. A 2024 study reported a range of plant compounds in the shrub, including flavonoids and other polyphenols, alkaloids and terpenoids, but that says more about the chemistry than about the drink's past.
